1.pericope_label: It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father's wife. And ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned, that he that hath done this deed might be taken away from among you.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin cover the publicity, the offence and the pride. Gill observes that the apostle, having reproved the Corinthians for their divisions about their ministers, proceeds to charge them with immoralities connived at among them, and particularly this notorious one; it was done not merely by one of their citizens or hearers but by one of their members, and so was cognizable by them as a church, since though they had nothing to do with them that were without they were concerned with them that were within. It was a public offence, known by everyone and in everybody's mouth, universally talked of and generally known at Corinth and in all Achaia, so that the church could not plead ignorance nor be excused from blame in not as publicly declaring their abhorrence of the fact. On their being puffed up Gill offers several possibilities: that they were elated with the gifts, learning and eloquence of their preachers and particularly of this man, who by some is thought to have been one of their teachers and was still cried up as a wonderful preacher; or that one party was puffed up against another, the opposite faction boasting over the man's own; or that they were puffed up with their own lenity and forbearance, boasting of it as humanity and an instance of charity; or else that they gloried in the thing itself as an instance of Christian liberty and freedom from the law, in which they might be strengthened by a Jewish notion that such things were lawful for proselyted Gentiles. Calvin holds that the contentions having originated in presumption, Paul appropriately proceeds to mention their diseases, the knowledge of which should humble them. Whether the man had seduced his father's wife as a prostitute or kept her under pretence of marriage is not certain, and does not much affect the subject in hand, since the former would be abominable whoredom and the latter an incestuous connection abhorrent to all propriety. That he may not seem to charge them on doubtful suspicions, Paul says the case is well known and in general circulation, the particle rendered commonly intimating that it was no vague rumour but a matter published everywhere so as to cause great scandal. Some, Calvin reports, infer from the mention of the Gentiles that Paul refers to the incest of Reuben and passed over Israel because a disgraceful instance had occurred there; this Calvin calls quite foreign to Paul's intention, since in mentioning the Gentiles rather than the Jews he designed to heighten the aggravation of the crime, and since the annals of the Gentiles record many such connections and tragedies have been founded upon them. What Paul means is that it was held in detestation among them as a shameful and abominable monstrosity, a beastly lust. On their glorying Calvin asks whether they were not ashamed to glory in what afforded so much occasion for humiliation, and asks further why they should grieve over another man's sin; he answers for two reasons, that in consequence of the communion existing among the members of the Church it was becoming that all should feel hurt at so deadly a fall on the part of one of their number, and that when such an enormity is perpetrated in a particular Church the whole society is in a manner polluted, as God's anger was kindled against the whole nation of Israel on account of the sacrilege of Achan.

Henry states the case and blames their conduct. The apostle lets them know what was the common report concerning them, that one of their community was guilty of fornication; it was told in all places to their dishonour and the reproach of Christians, and was the more reproachful because it could not be denied — the heinous sins of professed Christians being quickly noted and noised abroad, so that we should walk circumspectly, many eyes being upon us. This was not a common instance of fornication but such as was not so much as named among the Gentiles, that a man should have his father's wife, either marrying her while his father was alive or keeping her as his concubine, whether his father were dead or living. Had his father been dead and he married her after his decease, Henry allows, it had been incest still, but neither fornication nor adultery in the strictest sense; to marry her or keep her as a concubine while his father was alive, though he had repudiated her or she had deserted him, and whether she were his own mother or not, was incestuous fornication. Henry cites Cicero's description of an incredible wickedness, unheard of in all his life besides, when a woman had caused her daughter to be put away and was married to her husband; not that there were no such instances of incestuous marriages among the heathens, but whenever they happened they shocked every man of virtue and probity among them, who could not think of them without horror nor mention them without detestation. Yet such wickedness was committed by one in the church of Corinth, and, as is probable, by a leading man in one of the factions; the best churches, Henry concludes, are in this state of imperfection liable to very great corruptions.

Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Lightfoot supply the detail. Barnes notes that the report was heard, a rumour brought to Paul probably by the members of the family of Chloe, and that the word rendered commonly means everywhere, a matter of common fame. On their being puffed up he insists this does not mean they were proud on account of the wickedness, but that they were filled with pride notwithstanding it, when they ought to have been a troubled people who mourned and gave their first attention to removing the evil; men are always elated when they have the least occasion for it. He takes mourning in a large sense, of being so afflicted by the wickedness as to take the proper measures to remove the offender, and lays down that acts of discipline in the church should always commence with mourning that there is occasion for them, prompted not by anger, pride, revenge or party feeling but by deep grief and tender compassion for the offender; the taking away he understands of excommunication. Ellicott would render the opening There is absolutely said to be fornication among you, and such fornication as is not even among the Gentiles, noting that all the best manuscripts omit the word named, and that the force of the statement is that the fornication was of a kind which even the immoral Gentile world regarded with disgust. The word have, he adds, always implies in the New Testament actual marriage, so that she had probably been divorced from his father; and his father's wife is the Hebrew form of expression for stepmother, which Paul probably used instead of the ordinary Greek word because it was in this phraseology that such a union was forbidden by the law of Moses, though he quotes Chrysostom's suggestion that the phrase was chosen so as to strike much more severely. On the second verse Ellicott would read And are ye puffed up? as a question, and denies that the apostle can mean they actually gloried in the act of sin, referring their temper rather to the party rivalry described in the earlier chapters, when this common cause should have united them in one common grief. Robertson glosses the first adverb as wholly or altogether, possibly really or everywhere here; renders the verb literally it is heard, and follows Ellicott in supposing the household of Chloe brought the news. He notes the climactic qualitative pronoun showing the revolting character of the case, distinguishes the general word for such sin from the technical word for adultery on the part of the married, and calls the comparison with the Gentiles the height of scorn, since the very word Corinthianize meant to live in sexual wantonness and license. The construction, he says, means for one to go on having a wife of his father, probably a permanent union or concubinage without formal marriage, the woman probably a stepmother and the father possibly dead or divorced; the Jewish law prescribed stoning for this crime, but the rabbis invented a subterfuge in the case of a proselyte to permit such a relation, and perhaps the Corinthians had also learned how to split hairs over moral matters. On the second verse Robertson notes the emphatic position of the pronoun and the strong negative favouring a question, says the very least they could have done was to mourn for shame as if for one dead, and holds that decent self-respect should have compelled the instant expulsion of the man instead of pride in his rascality. Lightfoot argues that the woman was not the offender's own mother but the wife of his father, who seems from the second epistle to have been still alive: he that had done the wrong was plainly this incestuous person, and he that suffered the wrong was the father, without doubt then living, for it would scarcely have been said of him if dead that he suffered wrong by this wicked action. On the second verse Lightfoot sets out the rabbinic practice of reproof and excommunication, citing Rabbi Chasda that excommunication in Babylon answered to reproof in the land of Israel, and the cases of Bar Kaphra and of Rabbi Chaija, who taught in the street against Rabbi's order and drew his anger.

Clarke and Wesley take the offence and the remedy. Clarke holds that the word translated fornication must be understood in its utmost latitude of meaning, as implying all kinds of impurity, since the Corinthians were notoriously guilty of every species of irregularity and it is not likely that Paul would refer to only one. On the man's case he reports that commentators and critics have found great difficulties: one part is clear, that a man professing Christianity had illegal connections with his father's wife, but the principal question is whether the father was alive or dead. Most think he was alive and appeal to the second epistle, where the person who did the wrong is introduced along with him who suffered it; but after all that has been said Clarke thinks it most natural to conclude that the man had married the wife of his deceased father, not his own mother but a stepmother, then a widow. That this was not so much as named among the Gentiles must mean, he says, that it was not accredited by them, for it certainly did often occur; but their best writers who notice it brand it as superlatively infamous, Cicero styling it an incredible and unheard of wickedness. Clarke adds that the word named is wanting in almost every manuscript and version of importance. On their being puffed up he says they were full of strife and contention about their parties and favourite teachers and neglected the discipline of the Church; had they considered the greatness of the crime they would rather have mourned and put away the transgressor. The taking away he supposes is understood by some of the punishment of death and by others of excommunication, but holds that the Christian Church was at this time too young to have the forms of excommunication practised in succeeding centuries, and that probably no more is meant than a simple disowning of the person, with refusal to admit him to the sacred ordinances or to have any intercourse with him. Wesley glosses the original word as implying criminal conversation of any kind whatever, says of the father's wife that it was while his father was alive, and reads the second verse as a question: should they not rather have mourned, solemnly humbled themselves, and at that time of solemn mourning have expelled the notorious sinner from their communion?

Chrysostom examines the manner of the accusation. When Paul discoursed about their divisions he did not at once address them vehemently but more gently at first, ending in accusation; in this place, not so, but he lays about him immediately and makes the reproach of the accusation as general as possible. He said not, Why did such an one commit fornication? but, It is reported that there is fornication among you, that they might not as persons altogether aloof from his charge take it easily, but might be filled with such anxiety as was natural when the whole body was wounded and the Church had incurred reproach; for no one will state it thus, such an one hath committed fornication, but, in the Church of Corinthians that sin hath been committed. Nor did he say, Fornication is perpetrated, but, Is reported, such as is not even named among the Gentiles; for Paul continually makes the Gentiles a topic of reproach to the believers, as when he writes to the Thessalonians that every one should possess himself of his own vessel in sanctification, not in the passion of lust, even as the rest of the Gentiles, and to the Colossians and Ephesians that they should no longer walk as the other Gentiles walk. If their committing the same sins was unpardonable, Chrysostom asks, what place can be found for them when they outdid the Gentiles, among whom not only do they dare no such thing but they do not even give it a name. The clause among you he reads emphatically also: among you, the faithful, who have been favoured with so high mysteries, the partakers of secrets, the guests invited to heaven.

Tertullian, contending against an opponent who would divide the just God from the good, concedes the point of law here. He quite admits that, according to the Creator's law, the man was an offender who had his father's wife, and that the apostle in condemning him followed the principles of natural and public law.

debates: Whether the father was still living. Lightfoot argues from the second epistle that he was, since the man who suffered the wrong can only be the father and it would not be said of a dead man that he suffered wrong; Wesley asserts the same without argument; Clarke reports that most take that view but concludes the father was dead and the woman a widowed stepmother; Ellicott infers from the verb, which he says always means actual marriage, that she had been divorced from the father; Robertson denies any marriage at all and calls it concubinage, leaving the father dead or divorced; Henry admits either and distinguishes what each would make the crime; Calvin declines the question as not affecting the case.

How far the comparison with the Gentiles can be pressed. Chrysostom takes it at full strength, that the heathen do not even give the sin a name; Clarke, Henry and Calvin all qualify it, since such unions did occur among the heathen and were recorded in their annals and tragedies, so that Paul means only that the Gentiles held it in horror; Robertson turns the comparison on Corinth itself, whose name had become a byword for wantonness.

What their being puffed up refers to. Barnes holds that they were proud in spite of the scandal rather than because of it; Ellicott refers the pride to the earlier party rivalry and denies they gloried in the act; Robertson says the man's own faction justified him; Gill lists four possible objects of the pride, including a mistaken claim of Christian liberty; Calvin makes the grief they owed a matter of the communion of members and of the stain a church contracts.

What removing the man would have meant. Barnes and Wesley take it of excommunication and expulsion from communion; Clarke reports that some understood it of the death penalty, but judges the church too young for the later forms of excommunication and reduces it to a disowning with refusal of the ordinances; Robertson calls it instant expulsion; Lightfoot supplies the rabbinic background of reproof and excommunication.
outliers: Calvin alone refuses to decide the circumstances of the union, holding that whether it was prostitution or a pretended marriage leaves the offence equally execrable and the question therefore idle.
Robertson alone suggests that the Corinthians may have been imitating a rabbinic evasion, since the law prescribed stoning while the rabbis had contrived an exception for a proselyte.
themes: not so much as named among the Gentiles
he that hath done this deed

3.pericope_label: For I verily, as absent in body, but present in spirit, have judged already, as though I were present, concerning him that hath so done this deed, In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when ye are gathered together, and my spirit, with the power of our Lord Jesus Christ, To deliver such an one unto Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take opposite views of whose act this is. Gill notes that Paul, wherever he then was — at Philippi if the subscription of the epistle is to be trusted, or rather at Ephesus — was certainly not at Corinth. The naming of the Lord Jesus he takes to mean that the act would be done by his command, power and authority and for his glory, in whose name all miraculous actions were performed, this being one. On the delivering to Satan he is emphatic that it does not mean excommunication or the removing of the man from the communion of the church, which is an act of the whole church and not of any single person, and which the church had nothing to do with here: it was not what they were to do or ought to do, but what the apostle had resolved to do, an act of his own and peculiar to him as an apostle. Nor is the phrase a form of excommunication, nor was it ever so used by the primitive churches, nor ought it to be used now, since no man or set of men has power to do it after the ceasing of the extraordinary gifts of the Spirit, by which the apostles had power over Satan to dispossess him from the bodies of men. Calvin holds that, the Corinthians having been wanting in their duty, Paul now shows what ought to be done: excommunication, which they had sinfully delayed, is prescribed as the remedy for the disease, and in saying that he had already determined it he severely reproves their remissness, as though he said that they who had the thing every day before their eyes do nothing, while he for his part cannot endure it even at a distance. Lest any allege that he acted rashly in judging so far off, he declares himself present in spirit, meaning that the line of duty was as plain to him as if he saw the thing with his eyes. Calvin then draws out the mode of excommunication: Paul, though an Apostle, does not himself excommunicate according to his own pleasure but consults with the Church, that the matter may be transacted by common authority; he takes the lead and shows the way, but in taking others as his associates intimates plainly that this authority does not belong to any one individual. Since a multitude accomplishes nothing with moderation unless governed by counsel, there was appointed in the ancient Church a Presbytery, an assembly of elders who by the consent of all had the power of first judging the case, from whom the matter was brought before the people as a thing already judged; whatever the matter may be, any other course is contrary to the appointment of Christ and his Apostles and to the order of the Church. On the delivering to Satan Calvin reports that, since the Apostles had been furnished with the power of employing Satan as a scourge to correct the wicked and obstinate, some view these words as referring to a chastisement of that kind, as is usually said of the parallel passage concerning Alexander and Hymeneus, so that the phrase would mean nothing but the infliction of a severe punishment upon the body. But on examining the whole context more narrowly and comparing what is stated in the Second Epistle, Calvin gives up that interpretation as forced and at variance with Paul's meaning, and understands it simply of excommunication; for the phrase is an appropriate expression for denoting excommunication, since as Christ reigns within the Church so Satan reigns without it, as Augustine has remarked in his sixty-eighth sermon on the words of the Apostle. As we are received into the communion of the Church and remain in it on the condition that we are under the protection of Christ, he who is cast out of the Church is in a manner delivered over to the power of Satan, for he becomes an alien and is cast out of Christ's kingdom.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson supply the argument and the grammar. Barnes paraphrases the opening as Paul's declaration that whatever it may cost him, and whatever ill-will may result, he has adjudged the case so flagrant as to demand discipline, and since the church to whom it belongs has neglected it he uses the authority of an apostle and a spiritual father in directing it to take place; this was not a formal sentence of excommunication but the declared opinion of an apostle that such a sentence should be passed. On being present in spirit he reports that many suppose Paul refers to a power given to the apostles, though at a distance, to discern the real circumstances of a case by the gift of the Spirit, but holds that the phrase does not demand this interpretation and that Paul probably meant that though absent his mind and attention had been given to the subject. The naming of the Lord Jesus he takes of authority: the power to administer discipline is derived from Christ and is to be exercised in his name and for his honour; the assembly is to be gathered for the purpose of administering discipline and to act by that authority; and the mention of Paul's spirit means that, knowing his views and his love for them, they could act as if he were present, which Barnes says proves that discipline belongs to the church itself, so deep being Paul's conviction of it that even he would not administer it without them. On the delivering he reports that Beza and the Latin Fathers suppose this only an expression of excommunication, since the Scriptures recognise but two kingdoms, the kingdom of God or the church and the kingdom of the world under Satan, so that to exclude a man from one is to subject him to the other; Barnes finds some foundation for that opinion and no doubt that excommunication is intended, but holds that by being so placed the offender would be subject to corporal inflictions by the agency of Satan, here called the destruction of the flesh, Satan being elsewhere the author of bodily diseases as in the case of Job, and compares the delivering of Hymeneus and Alexander to Satan that they might learn not to blaspheme. Ellicott notes that the apostle had fully made up his mind that the offender must be removed and insists on the Corinthians doing it, so that the previous words imply they might as well have done it without waiting for his interference; he would omit the word rendered as, which is not in the best manuscripts; and on the last clause he states that the object of this punishment was the destruction of the flesh and the salvation of the man. Robertson marks the emphatic statement of Paul's own attitude in contrast with theirs, the concessive participles for being absent and being present, and the perfect indicative for a decision already reached; in a sentence of much difficulty Paul seems to conceive an imaginary church court in which the culprit has been tried and condemned, and there are various ways of punctuating the clauses. The genitive absolute for their being gathered together in regular assembly, with Paul's spirit, meeting in the name of the Lord Jesus, may take the clause about the power of the Lord Jesus either with itself or with the infinitive to deliver, both making good syntax and sense, the chief difference being that on the former reading Paul assumes less apostolic prerogative to himself. On the delivering Robertson notes the same idiom used of Hymenius and Alexander, and Paul's own physical suffering described as a messenger of Satan; he takes it certainly of expulsion from the church and of regarding the man as outside the commonwealth of Israel, but denies that expulsion from a local church means the damnation of the offender, since wilful offenders are to be expelled and not regarded as enemies but admonished as brothers. The destruction of the flesh he takes both of physical suffering, as in the case of Job, and of the conquest of the fleshly sins, remedial punishment; the salvation of the spirit is the ultimate purpose of the expulsion as discipline, Paul's motive being not vindictive but the reformation of the offender, and the final salvation of the man in the day of Christ the goal, to be attained not by condoning his sin.

Clarke and Wesley both suppose a miraculous element. Clarke thinks Paul may refer to the gift of the discernment of spirits, which the apostles in general very likely possessed on extraordinary occasions, having already seen the matter so clearly that he had determined what punishment should be inflicted; the naming of the Lord Jesus he takes of the head of the Church, under whose authority every act is to be performed, and Paul's spirit of his apostolical authority derived from him, with the miraculous energy of the Lord Jesus to inflict the punishment the Corinthians pronounce. On the delivering to Satan Clarke states that there is no evidence that this was any form of excommunication known either among the Jews or the Christians, and that those who have searched all the Jewish records, among them Selden and Schoettgen, have found nothing that answers to it. It was a species of punishment administered in extraordinary cases, in which the body and mind of an incorrigible transgressor were delivered by the authority of God into the power of Satan, to be tortured with diseases and terrors as a warning to all; but while body and mind were thus tormented the immortal spirit was under the influence of the Divine mercy, and the affliction was in general only for a season, though sometimes evidently unto death, as the destruction of the flesh seems to imply. The soul found mercy at the hand of God, for such an extraordinary interference of God's power and justice and of Satan's influence could not fail to bring the person to the deepest humiliation and contrition, so that while the flesh was destroyed the spirit was saved in the day of the Lord Jesus. No such power as this remains in the Church of God, Clarke insists; none such should be assumed, and the pretensions to it are as wicked as they are vain. It was the same power by which Ananias and Sapphira were struck dead and Elymas the sorcerer struck blind, and apostles alone were entrusted with it. Wesley reads the first clause of a full and, it seems, miraculous view of the whole fact, so that Paul judged as if actually present; the mention of his spirit he takes as present with them, and the power of the Lord Jesus as confirming his sentence. The delivering he calls the highest degree of punishment in the Christian church, and observes that the passing of this sentence was the act of the apostle and not of the Corinthians; Satan was usually permitted in such cases to inflict pain or sickness on the offender, and the destruction of the flesh proceeded slowly and gradually, unless prevented by speedy repentance.

debates: What being present in spirit means. Clarke and Wesley suppose a miraculous discernment granted to the apostles on extraordinary occasions; Barnes reports that reading and declines it, taking Paul to mean only that his mind had been given to the case; Calvin reaches the same modest sense, that the duty was as plain to him as if seen with his eyes; Robertson describes instead a legal fiction, an imaginary church court in which the man has been tried.

Whose act the sentence is. Barnes takes the passage to prove that discipline belongs to the church itself, since even an apostle would not act without them, and Calvin builds the ancient Presbytery on the same clause, denying that the authority belongs to any individual; Gill holds the delivering to Satan to be the apostle's own act and no part of the church's business at all, and Wesley says the same; Robertson locates the difference in the punctuation, since on one reading of the clause about the Lord's power Paul assumes less prerogative to himself.

What delivering to Satan is. Calvin reports the reading that makes it bodily chastisement and rejects it as forced, taking it simply of excommunication, since Satan reigns outside the Church as Christ reigns within; Barnes reports Beza and the Latin fathers to the same effect and accepts excommunication, but adds that the man was thereby exposed to bodily infliction; Clarke denies flatly that any such form of excommunication was known to Jews or Christians and makes it an extraordinary apostolic punishment; Gill agrees with Clarke and adds that the phrase ought never to be used now.

What the destruction of the flesh accomplishes. Clarke has diseases and terrors that bring the man to humiliation, generally for a season though sometimes unto death; Wesley makes it slow and gradual and stoppable by speedy repentance; Robertson takes it both of physical suffering and of the conquest of fleshly sin, remedial and not vindictive; Ellicott states only the object, the destruction of the flesh and the salvation of the man.
outliers: Clarke alone rests his case on a negative documentary result, that those who ransacked the Jewish records found nothing answering to this form of sentence, and alone declares that the pretension to such a power now is as wicked as it is vain.
Calvin alone turns the clause about the assembly into a question of polity, deriving from it the ancient assembly of elders that judged first and then laid the matter before the people.
themes: I verily, as absent in body
him that hath so done this deed
in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ
the power of our Lord Jesus Christ
to deliver such an one unto Satan
that the spirit may be saved
the day of the Lord Jesus

6.pericope_label: Your glorying is not good. Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump? Purge out therefore the old leaven, that ye may be a new lump, as ye are unleavened. For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us: Therefore let us keep the feast, not with old leaven, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness; but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the glorying, the purging and the feast. Gill refers their glorying to their outward flourishing condition, their riches and wealth, and their ministers, their wisdom and parts, when under such a humbling dispensation; and especially if they gloried in the sin itself and their connivance at it, it was far from good but very criminal, and dangerous in its consequence. On the purging he offers two senses: either the incestuous person, whose crime might well be compared to sour leaven and called old because of his long continuance in it, whom the apostle would have removed, which is properly the act of excommunication that the church was to perform and quite distinct from what the apostle himself determined to do; or an exhortation to the church in general, themselves as well as this man, to relinquish their old course of sinning and put off the former conversation, it being usual with the Jews to call the corruption of nature leaven in the lump. The allusion, he says, is to the strict search the Jews made just before their passover, that no leaven might remain when the feast began, made by the light of a lamp on the night of the fourteenth of Nisan in every secret place, hole and corner of the house. On the feast Gill denies that the feast of the passover is meant, which was now ceased, though the words are said in allusion to it. Calvin condemns their glorying not simply because they extolled themselves beyond what is lawful for man but because they delighted themselves in their faults: he had previously shown that men owe the praise of any excellence to God alone, whereas what he treats here is that the Corinthians were guilty of arrant folly in extolling themselves without just ground, proudly glorying as if everything had been in a golden style among them while so much among them was wicked and disgraceful. Lest they should think it a matter of little importance that they gave encouragement to so great an evil, he shows the destructive tendency of indulgence and dissimulation, using a proverbial saying by which he intimates that a whole multitude is infected by the contagion of a single individual. Having borrowed the similitude, Calvin says, Paul pursues it farther and makes a transition from a particular point to a general doctrine, no longer speaking of the case of incest but exhorting them generally to purity of life, on the ground that we cannot remain in Christ if we are not cleansed; and Calvin remarks on the exquisite skill of the transition, which he compares to the fine transitions of the odes of Pindar, bold and surprising yet perfectly natural. On the feast he says that as the outward passover was to the fathers a figure of the true, so its appendages were figures of the reality we possess, and that we shall be members of Christ only when we have renounced malice and deceit. He observes further that the ancient passover was not merely a memorial of a past benefit but also a sacrament representing the Christ who was to come, from whom we have the privilege of passing from death to life, since otherwise it would not hold good that in Christ is the substance of the legal shadows; and he uses the passage to set aside the sacrilege of the Papal mass, since Paul does not teach that Christ is offered daily.

Henry exhorts them to purity by purging out the old leaven, and takes the advice as addressed either to the church in general or to each member. Addressed to the church, purging out the old leaven that they might be a new lump refers to putting away from themselves that wicked person; Christian churches should be pure and holy and not bear such corrupt and scandalous members, being unleavened and enduring no such heterogeneous mixture to sour and corrupt them. Addressed to each particular member, it implies that they should purge themselves from all impurity of heart and life, especially from the kind of wickedness to which the Corinthians were addicted to a proverb; Christians should be careful to keep themselves clean as well as purge polluted members out of their society, and should especially avoid the sins to which they were once most addicted and the reigning vices of the places and people where they live. They were also to purge themselves from malice and wickedness, all ill-will and mischievous subtlety, which Henry calls leaven that sours the mind to a great degree, and thinks it not improbable that this was intended as a check to some who gloried.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson supply the argument, the occasion and the philology. Barnes glosses their glorying as confidence in their present condition as if they were eminent in purity and piety, and says boasting is never good but is especially wrong when an existing evil is likely to corrupt the whole church; when men are disposed to boast they should inquire whether there is not some sin on account of which they should be humbled, and it is only when we are blind to the realities of the case that we are disposed to boast. The proverb of the leaven he notes occurs also in Galatians, and by leaven the Hebrews metaphorically understood whatever had the power of corrupting, whether doctrine or example. On the purging he takes the figure from the custom of the Jews at the passover, who searched every part of their dwellings with candles that they might remove every particle of leavened bread, and so exhorts the Corinthians to use all diligence to search out and remove all sin; by the old leaven he means vice and sin, and also the person who had committed the sin in their church; that ye may be a new lump means that they may be like a new mass of dough before the leaven is put in; and as ye are unleavened means as they are bound by their Christian profession to be. On the feast he says the language is drawn from the paschal feast and does not mean literally the paschal supper, which had ceased to be observed by Christians, nor the Lord's Supper particularly, but that as the Jews put away all leaven as emblematic of sin, so Christians in the slaying of their sacrifice should put away all wickedness from their hearts as individuals and from their societies and churches. The leaven of malice he glosses as unkindness and evil which would diffuse itself and invade the mass of Christians, and the word for wickedness as sin or evil generally, with particular reference to the case of the incestuous person. Ellicott suspects a reference to some boasting about their spiritual state contained in the letter which had reached Paul from Corinth: so long as that one bad person is among them it gives a bad character to the whole community, as leaven, though it may not have pervaded the entire lump, still makes it not the unleavened bread necessary for the Paschal Feast. This Epistle being written shortly before Pentecost, he judges it was very likely about or soon after Easter, so that the leaven and the Paschal Feast naturally suggest themselves as illustrations, the Apostle passing rapidly from the mention of the leaven to the whole scene of the feast: as with the most minute and scrupulous care the Jew would remove every atom of leaven when the Paschal lamb was to be eaten, so our Paschal Lamb having been slain we must take care that no moral leaven remains in the sacred household of the Church while she keeps her perpetual feast of prayer and thanksgiving. On the purging Ellicott insists that it is not the offending man who is here spoken of but the spirit in the Church which tolerated the evil, which is to be purged out of their midst that they may become actually a new lump as they are by profession unleavened. He would render the next clause Christ our passover is slain, noting that the words for us are not in the best manuscripts and that the word translated sacrifice is generally used in the New Testament in the sense simply of slaying or killing. The old leaven he takes of their old state generally, sincerity and truth being to take the place of malice and wickedness in the continuous life of the Christian; and he approves the remark that the whole of time is a festival unto Christians because of the excellence of the good things given. Robertson glosses the word for not good as not beautiful or seemly in view of this plague spot, a cancer on the church needing a surgical operation at once instead of boasting. He notes the proverb also in Galatians, derives the word for leaven from the verb to boil, points to the parables of Jesus for the pervasive power of leaven, and remarks that some of the members may have argued that one such case did not affect the church as a whole, a specious excuse for negligence that Paul answers; the emphasis is on the word little, and the word for lump means a substance mixed with water and kneaded like dough, so that he compares the pervasive power of germs of disease spreading through the body. The imperative to purge out is an effective aorist of urgency, to do it now and do it before the whole church is contaminated, the metaphor being from the command to purge out the old and decayed leaven before the passover feast, and he compares modern methods of disinfection after a contagious disease. A new lump means a fresh start as a new community with the contamination removed, and he distinguishes the word for new as not yet old from the word meaning fresh as compared with the ancient; unleavened is the normal and ideal state of Christians, a rare word among the ancients, and he quotes the comment that Christians are a new creation, exemplifying the maxim that you should treat a man as if he were what you would wish him to be. On the feast he reads the present subjunctive as let us keep on keeping the feast, a perpetual feast, and keep the leaven out; it is quite possible that Paul was writing about the time of the Jewish passover, since it was before Pentecost, but if so that is merely incidental and his language here is not a plea for the observance of Easter by Christians. He glosses the leaven of malice and wickedness as vicious disposition and evil deed, notes that there is no word for bread in the last clause, and traces the word for sincerity to the notion of judging by the light of the sun and the word for truth to what is unconcealed, the Greek idea of truth being out in the open.

Clarke and Wesley apply it. Clarke says they were triumphing in their superior knowledge and busy setting up their respective teachers while the Church was left under the most scandalous corruptions, and asks whether with all their boasted wisdom they do not acknowledge the truth of the common maxim; if the leaven, the incestuous person, be permitted to remain and his conduct not exposed by the most formidable censure, the flood-gates of impurity will be opened on the Church and the whole state of Christianity ruined in Corinth. On the purging he says that, as it is the custom of the Jews before the passover to search their houses in the most diligent manner for the old leaven and throw it out, sweeping every part clean, so they are to act with this incestuous person, and he refers to his notes on Exodus for the care with which the Jews purged their houses. On the feast he judges it very likely that the time of the passover was now approaching, when the Church would be called to extraordinary acts of devotion in commemorating the passion, death and resurrection of Christ, and that the apostle takes advantage of the circumstance. Under the Christian dispensation, he says, we must be saved equally from Judaism, heathenism and sin of every kind; malice and wickedness must be destroyed and sincerity and truth take their place. Clarke refers the words not more to wicked principles than to wicked men: not with the old leaven, the impure principles that actuated them in their heathen state, neither with the leaven of malice and wickedness, that is radical depravity producing unrighteousness in the life, nor with the persons thus influenced, but with the unleavened bread, that is with upright and godly men who have such purity of affections and conduct that even the light of God shining upon them discovers no flaw, and who are inwardly as well as outwardly what they profess to be. He observes that the word translated wickedness is very like the word for fornication. Wesley refers the glorying to their gifts or prosperity at such a time as this, glosses a little leaven as one sin or one sinner and the leavening of the lump as diffusing guilt and infection through the whole congregation, and takes the purging of both sinners and sin. On the passover he says the Jewish passover was only a type of this, and exclaims at the exquisite skill which here and everywhere conducts the zeal of the inspired writer, so surprising a transition and yet so perfectly natural, the apostle speaking of the incestuous criminal and sliding into his darling topic, a crucified Saviour. On the feast he says let us feed on him by faith, finding here a plain allusion to the Lord's supper, which was instituted in the room of the passover; the old leaven he takes of heathenism or Judaism, malignity as stubbornness in evil, and sincerity and truth as put for the whole of true inward religion.

debates: What is to be purged out. Clarke reads the command straight at the incestuous man; Ellicott denies that the man is in view at all and makes it the spirit in the Church that tolerated him; Barnes takes it of both the sin and the sinner; Gill sets out the two senses without choosing between them; Henry divides it between the body's duty to expel and each member's duty to cleanse himself; Calvin holds that Paul has left the particular case behind for a general exhortation.

Whether Paul wrote at passover time. Clarke thinks the season was approaching and that Paul took advantage of it; Ellicott reasons from the letter's date before Pentecost that it was about or soon after Easter, which suggested the figures; Robertson allows the possibility but insists it is incidental and refuses to let the verse become a plea for keeping Easter.

What keeping the feast now means. Gill denies the passover is meant, since it had ceased; Barnes denies both the paschal supper and the Lord's Supper in particular and makes it the putting away of all evil; Wesley finds the Lord's Supper plainly here and reads the feast as feeding on Christ by faith; Robertson takes the tense as continuous, a perpetual feast; Calvin uses the verse to deny that Christ is offered daily.

What the unleavened bread stands for. Barnes and Wesley take it of inward religion, sincerity and truth against malice and wickedness; Clarke reads it of persons, upright and godly men in whom the light of God discovers no flaw; Robertson notes there is no word for bread at all and glosses the pair as vicious disposition and evil deed.
outliers: Robertson alone refuses the inference the imagery invites, granting that Paul may have written near the passover while denying that anything follows from it for Christian observance.

Calvin and Wesley alone attend to the artistry of the passage rather than its argument, both admiring the transition from the incestuous man to the crucified Saviour and both reaching for the odes of Pindar to describe it.
themes: that ye may be a new lump
Christ our passover is sacrificed for us
the leaven of malice and wickedness
the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth

9.pericope_label: I wrote unto you in an epistle not to company with fornicators: Yet not altogether with the fornicators of this world, or with the covetous, or extortioners, or with idolaters; for then must ye needs go out of the world. But now I have written unto you not to keep company, if any man that is called a brother be a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, or a drunkard, or an extortioner; with such an one no not to eat.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the letter, the limitation and the grammar. Gill holds that the epistle referred to is not this one but some other sent before, which either came not to hand or was neglected by them, so that what is said here may be considered a reproof for taking no notice of his advice while continuing to show respect to the incestuous person. No doubt the apostle wrote other epistles besides those in being, and such a supposition does not detract from the perfection of Scripture, for not all that he wrote was by divine inspiration, and as many as were so and were necessary for the canon have been preserved; nor does it contradict this epistle's being his first to the church, for though it might not be his first to them it is the first to us. By the fornicators of this world Gill understands men of the world, mere worldly carnal men never called out of it, as distinct from those in the church who had committed the same sin; the former prohibition was not to be understood as forbidding all civil conversation and commerce with such, nor with the covetous, or extortioners, or idolaters of this world, the qualification applying to each. The covetous he takes either of those given up to inordinate lusts who work all uncleanness with greediness, or of those greedily desirous of increasing their worldly substance by any method, right or wrong. On the next verse he notes that the words show what he had written before was at another time and in another epistle, though what he now writes is not different from it, only an explanation of the persons meant and the thing enjoined. Calvin states plainly that the epistle spoken of is not at this day extant, and that many others are lost, but that it is enough that those have been preserved which the Lord foresaw would suffice; the passage, he says, has in consequence of its obscurity been twisted to a variety of interpretations. The word rendered to company means to be on terms of familiarity and close intimacy, and Paul's reminding them of the injunction exposes their remissness, since they had been admonished and had remained inactive. On the limitation Calvin reports that interpreters are not agreed: some say the sense is that they must sooner quit Greece; Ambrose says they must rather die; Erasmus turns it into the optative, as if Paul wished they might leave the world altogether but, being unable, must at least quit the society of those who falsely assume the name of Christians while exhibiting the worst example. Chrysostom's exposition, Calvin judges, has more appearance of truth: that in commanding them to shun fornicators Paul does not mean all such, otherwise they would have to go in quest of another world, since we must live among thorns so long as we sojourn on earth, but requires only that they not keep company with fornicators who wish to be regarded as brethren, lest they should seem by their sufferance to approve of their wickedness; the term world is accordingly to be taken of the present life, as in the Lord's prayer that the Father would not take them out of the world. On the last verse Calvin notes that in the Greek there is a participle without a verb according to the common reading, while a number of manuscripts, versions and editions supply one, which he thinks rightly done; those who view the clause as referring to what follows bring out a forced meaning at variance with Paul's intention, though Calvin confesses the sentiment they draw from it is just and worthy of notice, that no one can be punished by the decision of the Church but one whose sin has become matter of notoriety.

Henry takes the advice as counsel to shun the company and converse of scandalous professors. Some think the letter mentioned was written to them before and is lost; yet we have lost nothing by it, the Christian revelation being entire in those books of scripture which have come down to us, which are all that were intended by God for the general use of Christians, since otherwise he could and would in his providence have preserved more of the writings of inspired men. Others think it is to be understood of this very epistle, that Paul had written this advice before he had full information of their whole case but thought it needful now to be more particular. On that occasion he tells them that if any man called a brother, professing Christianity and being a member of a Christian church, were a fornicator, or covetous, or an idolater, or a railer, they should not keep company with him nor so much as eat with him, avoiding all familiarity and having no commerce with him.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson weigh the evidence. Barnes notes that the verb may refer either to this epistle or to some former one and does not decide the question by itself, and sets out the parties: a large number of commentators, among them Chrysostom, Theodoret and Oecumenius, most of the Latin commentators and nearly all the Dutch, suppose the reference is to this same epistle, taking the article for a demonstrative and appealing to kindred passages in Romans, Colossians and the Thessalonian epistles; many others, among them Grotius, Doddridge and Rosenmuller, suppose it refers to another epistle now lost, which might have been very brief and contained little more than this direction, and Barnes holds this the correct opinion. On the limitation he explains that Paul did not mean they should refuse all kinds of intercourse, or decline to treat such men with civility or to be engaged with them in the transactions of life, for this would be impossible, but that they should not so associate as to be esteemed to belong to them or to be corrupted by their example: they were not to make them companions and friends. Most heathen, he adds, were of this description and particularly at Corinth, and all the Corinthians before the gospel was preached there worshipped idols, so that to avoid them all would require leaving the world. On the next verse he takes the idolater to mean those who while professing Christianity still attended the idol feasts and worshipped there, perhaps a few hypocrites, and the railer to be a reproachful man of coarse and bitter words whose characteristic was to abuse others, which he observes is contrary to the example of the Master, who when he was reviled reviled not again. Ellicott reports the controversy whether a former unpreserved epistle is meant or this one, notes the suggestion that the words may have been added as an interpolation after the completion of the epistle to intensify the earlier remarks, and calls such an interpretation rather strained; it is more natural to suppose an epistle written to the Corinthians, probably from Ephesus, after a visit paid to Corinth of which there is no record, since a third visit is contemplated in the second epistle whereas only one previous one is recorded, and the condition of the Church which caused the apostle that heaviness would naturally have given rise to such a letter. On the limitation Ellicott explains that it would have been almost impossible for the command to be literally obeyed without the Christian withdrawing altogether from the business of life, so that what the Apostle is anxious to preserve is the fair fame and purity of the Church: there are so many fornicators and covetous and idolaters in the heathen world that men must meet with them, but Christians must tolerate no such sins among themselves and must exclude from the social circle any brother who, bearing the name of Christ, indulges in the vices of the heathen world, the Church being the light of the world and not the recipient of the world's darkness. On the catalogue he observes that it may seem strange that idolater should be included, since in what sense could a brother be a worshipper of idols, and judges that the word probably involves not merely the worshipping of an image but the sensuality which accompanied various forms of heathen worship. Robertson denies that the first verb is an epistolary aorist and takes it of an epistle earlier than this one and not preserved to us, asking what a find it would be if a bundle of papyri in Egypt should give it back; the verb rendered to have no company is a late double compound used in the papyri for mixing up with. On the limitation he notes that the phrase means not absolutely, not in all circumstances, so that Paul confines the prohibition to members of the church and has no jurisdiction over outsiders. The covetous he glosses as the over-reachers, those avaricious for more and more, a word that always comes in bad company with the licentious and the idolaters; the extortioners as a rapacious adjective used as a substantive, whom he would call bandits or grafters today; and the idolaters as hirelings of the idols. On the last verse he says the aorist there is epistolary and refers to this same epistle, unlike the earlier one, and that the condition is a supposable case; he notes the words for reviler and drunkard, cites Deissmann for a list of virtues and vices on counters for Roman games corresponding remarkably with Paul's list, and records that Chrysostom noted people in his day complaining of the bad company Paul gives revilers and drunkards, as men with more respectable vices.

Clarke and Wesley stand apart on the letter and together on the practice. Clarke holds that the wisest and best skilled in Biblical criticism agree that the apostle does not refer to any other epistle than this, and that he speaks of general directions given in the foregoing part of it which he now changes and greatly strengthens; the words may be translated I had written to you in this epistle, since there are many instances in the New Testament where the aorist is used for the perfect and the pluperfect, and Whitby produces several proofs, contending that the conclusion drawn by some that it refers to a lost epistle is not legitimately drawn from the text or from antiquity. The principal evidence against this, Clarke concedes, is the parallel phrase in the second epistle, which appears to refer to this first one; and he allows that possibly the apostle refers to an epistle written though not sent, suppressed when he received further information from Stephanas, Fortunatus and Achaicus about the state of the Corinthian Church. On the limitation Clarke exclaims at the awful picture of the general corruption of manners, since the Christians at Corinth could not transact the ordinary affairs of life with any others than fornicators, covetous persons, extortioners, railers, drunkards and idolaters, because there were none others in the place; how necessary was Christianity in that city. On the last verse he adds that a man may transact his worldly concerns with a person who knows not God and makes no profession of Christianity, whatever his moral character, but must not so far acknowledge a man professing Christianity who is scandalous in his conduct: let him have this extra mark of abhorrence of all sin, and let the world see that the Church of God does not tolerate iniquity. Wesley takes it of a former epistle, adding that doubtless both Paul and the other apostles wrote many things not extant now, and glosses the prohibition as forbidding familiar conversation and any intimacy beyond what is absolutely necessary. On the limitation he says Paul did not mean they should altogether refrain from conversing with heathens though guilty in some of these respects, classifies the covetous, rapacious and idolaters as sinners against themselves, their neighbour and God, and observes that going out of the world, which some account a perfection, Paul accounts an utter absurdity, since then all civil commerce must cease. On the last verse he glosses the brother as a Christian and especially a member of the same congregation, the rapacious as guilty of oppression, extortion or any open injustice, and the refusal to eat as withholding the lowest degree of familiarity.

Chrysostom explains why the qualification was necessary. Since Paul had said that they had not mourned that such an one should be taken away, and had told them to purge out the old leaven, it was likely they would surmise it their duty to avoid all fornicators; for if he that has sinned imparts some of his own mischief to those who have not sinned, much more is it meet to keep away from those without, and if one ought not to spare a friend on account of such mischief arising from him, much less any others. Under this impression it was probable they would separate themselves from the fornicators among the Greeks also, and the matter thus turning out impossible they would have taken it more to heart. He therefore used this mode of correction, saying that he wrote to them to have no company with fornicators, yet not altogether with the fornicators of this world, using the word altogether as if it were an acknowledged thing; and that they might not think he charged this on them as being rather imperfect, and attempt it under the erroneous impression that they were perfect, he shows that this were even impossible to be done though they wished it ever so much, since it would be necessary to seek another world.

debates: Which epistle is meant. Calvin, Robertson, Wesley and Gill all take it of an earlier letter now lost, Gill adding that its loss leaves the perfection of Scripture untouched and Henry that nothing needful was lost with it; Ellicott places that letter after an unrecorded visit and rejects the theory of an interpolation; Barnes lays out the two parties by name and decides for the lost letter; Clarke denies the whole account, reads the aorist as a pluperfect referring to this epistle, and holds the inference of a lost letter illegitimate, though he concedes the second epistle tells against him.

What the qualification concedes. Chrysostom holds Paul is showing the stricter course impossible, since it would require another world; Calvin reports readings that make it quitting Greece, or dying, or a wish of Erasmus that they could leave the world, and prefers Chrysostom's; Barnes and Ellicott make it a matter of ordinary business that cannot be avoided; Robertson makes it a question of jurisdiction over members rather than outsiders; Wesley calls withdrawal from the world an utter absurdity.

How a brother could be an idolater. Ellicott finds the word strange in the list and supposes it carries the sensuality attending heathen worship; Barnes takes it of professing Christians who still attended the idol feasts.

What the refusal to eat covers. Clarke extends it to communion in things either sacred or civil, and contrasts the liberty a Christian has in worldly dealings with an open unbeliever; Wesley calls eating together the lowest degree of familiarity; Henry joins the two, that they were to keep no company and have no commerce with such a man.
outliers: Clarke alone holds out against the consensus that a lost epistle is in view, resting on the aorist's use for the pluperfect and on the authority of Whitby, and alone proposes that the letter may have been written and then suppressed.
Calvin alone canvasses the older interpretations of the concession one by one, weighing Ambrose and Erasmus against Chrysostom before adopting the last.
themes: I wrote unto you in an epistle
then must ye needs go out of the world
any man that is called a brother
with such an one no not to eat

12.pericope_label: For what have I to do to judge them also that are without? do not ye judge them that are within? But them that are without God judgeth. Therefore put away from among yourselves that wicked person.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the jurisdiction and the sentence. Gill glosses judging as admonishing, reproving, censuring and condemning, and says that God will judge those without in the great day, so that although such persons did not fall under the censures and punishment of the apostle or of a church of Christ they shall not go unpunished, but will be called to account for their fornication, covetousness, idolatry and extortion and judged according to their works; since they do not fall under the cognizance of the churches of Christ they are to be left to the tribunal of God, and all that the saints have to do is to watch over one another and reprove, rebuke and censure as cases require, as the case of this church did. Calvin denies that outsiders are altogether beyond judgment: there is nothing to hinder us from judging these also, and even devils themselves are not exempt from the judgment of the word which is committed to us; but Paul is speaking here of the jurisdiction that belongs peculiarly to the Church, since the Lord has furnished us with this power that we may exercise it upon those who belong to his household, this chastisement being a part of discipline confined to the Church and not extending to strangers. We do not therefore pronounce their condemnation, because the Lord has not subjected them to our cognisance and jurisdiction so far as chastisement and censure are concerned, and we are constrained to leave them to the judgment of God; it is in this sense that Paul speaks, since God allows them to wander about unbridled like wild beasts, there being no one who can restrain their wantonness. On the closing sentence Calvin reports that it is commonly explained as referring to the person guilty of the illicit connection, and observes that those who understand the expression to mean putting away the wicked thing are refuted by the Greek words Paul uses, the article being in the masculine gender. But he asks what if it should be viewed as referring to the devil, who undoubtedly, in the person of a wicked and unprincipled man allowed to continue, is encouraged to establish his throne among us; for the wicked one, taken simply and without any addition, denotes the prince of all crimes rather than some wicked man.

Barnes, Ellicott, Robertson and Lightfoot divide over the sense of the question. Barnes says Paul has no authority over those outside and can exercise no jurisdiction over them, so that all his rules must have reference only to those within the church; to judge is to pass sentence upon, to condemn or to punish, and those without are outside the pale of the Christian church, heathens and men of the world who did not profess to be Christians. He asks whether their jurisdiction as Christians is not confined to those within and professed members of it, and whether they ought not to exercise discipline there and separate unworthy persons from their society, as in this instance. On the last verse he says those unconnected with the church are under the direct and peculiar government of God: they are indeed sinners and deserve punishment, but it is not ours to pronounce sentence or inflict punishment, our province being the church, and all others we are to leave entirely in God's hands. Since it is theirs to judge the members of their own society, they are to exercise discipline on the offender and put him away; excommunication is the utmost power the church has, and this the church is bound to exercise on all who have openly offended against the laws of Christ. Ellicott says the apostle in this verse at once explains the grounds of the limitation of his remarks to Christians and seems to hint, by the form of expression, that the Corinthian Church ought to have been able to understand his remarks as applicable only to themselves and not to the heathen; those without means the heathen, a common form of expression among the Jews to designate the Gentile world. As the Christian Church could sit in judgment only on its own members, so they should have concluded that only on those had Paul passed judgment. On the last verse he notes that in the best manuscripts the verb is in the future tense, God will judge, that he is the judge of the whole earth and we are to leave the heathen world in his hands; he would omit the word therefore, and observes that the Apostle adopts the form of pronouncing sentence on great criminals with which especially the Jewish converts would be familiar from Deuteronomy. Robertson glosses the question as asking what it is to Paul to judge those without, since they are outside the church and not within his jurisdiction and God passes judgment on them; and he says that by the quotation from Deuteronomy Paul clinches the case for the expulsion of the offender, noting the effective aorist. Lightfoot alone sticks at the version and sense commonly received. He records that Beza reads what doth it concern me, the French what have I to do to judge, and the Italian what doth it belong to me to judge, and knows well enough that the Greek phrase very frequently occurs in that sense; but he asks on good ground that if it concerns the blessed apostle not to judge them that are without, why did he judge Elymas with blindness, and why Hymeneus and Alexander by delivering them into the hands of Satan, when they were now apostates and no other than such as were without. He therefore proposes that the words be rendered to this sense: for why is power granted me to judge concerning them also that are without, that is, by apostolic authority to strike even a heathen with some divine plague if he be incorrigible.

Clarke and Wesley state the rule and the text. Clarke explains that those without signifies persons who were not members of the Church, and that the corresponding Hebrew term is generally so understood in the Jewish writers, where it frequently occurs. The word rendered also, which he says greatly disturbs the sense here, is wanting in a number of manuscripts and in the Syriac, Coptic, Slavonic, Vulgate and Itala, together with several of the fathers; with that word omitted the sentence should stand thus: Does it belong to me to pass sentence on those which are without, which are not members of the Church? By no means. Pass ye sentence on them which are within, which are members of the Church; those which are not members God will pass sentence on, in that way in which he generally deals with the heathen world. But put ye away the evil from among yourselves — in which last clause Clarke finds an allusion to Deuteronomy, where the like directions are given to the congregation of Israel relative to a person found guilty of idolatry. Wesley says Paul speaks of Christians only and asks what he has to do to judge heathens, since they, as well as he, judge those of their own community; the passing of sentence on those without God has reserved to himself, and the taking away of the wicked person properly belongs to them.

debates: Whether the question disclaims a power or asks after one. Barnes, Robertson, Ellicott and Wesley all read it as a disclaimer of jurisdiction over outsiders; Calvin accepts the disclaimer but limits it to chastisement and censure, holding that nothing hinders us from judging outsiders by the word; Lightfoot rejects the received rendering altogether and, appealing to Elymas and to Hymeneus and Alexander, would translate it as asking why the apostle has power to judge those without at all.

Whether the word rendered also belongs in the text. Clarke reports that it is wanting in many manuscripts and versions and says it greatly disturbs the sense, reading the verse without it as a plain question and denial; Lightfoot, keeping it, finds in the resulting sense the very difficulty that drives him to a new rendering.

What is to become of those outside. Gill and Wesley leave them to the judgment of the great day, which God has reserved to himself; Barnes says they are under God's direct and peculiar government and are not ours to sentence; Ellicott prefers the future reading, God will judge, and leaves the heathen world in the hands of the judge of all the earth; Calvin describes them meanwhile as wandering unbridled like wild beasts, with none to restrain them.

Who the wicked person is. Barnes, Robertson, Clarke and Wesley all take it of the offender and read the clause as the sentence of expulsion, Robertson and Clarke both tracing the words to the command given to Israel in Deuteronomy; Calvin, having refuted the neuter reading on grammatical grounds, suggests that the phrase may denote the devil, who sets up his throne where a wicked man is tolerated.
outliers: Lightfoot alone measures the verse against the apostle's recorded conduct and finds the usual translation contradicted by it, preferring a rendering that grants Paul power over outsiders rather than denying it.
Calvin alone proposes that what is to be put away is not the man but the prince of all crimes, arguing from the bare use of the wicked one without any addition.
themes: what have I to do to judge
do not ye judge them that are within
